entry.title: TypeScript Advanced Patterns: Writing Cleaner & Safer Code in 2025
Docker Series: Episode 20 — Docker Security Best Practices & Secrets Management 🔒
entry.summary:
Welcome back! In previous episodes, we covered Docker Compose, Networking, Swarm, and Volumes. Now it’s time to focus on security — protecting your containers, images, and sensitive information. Containers are isolated, but misconfigurations can expose vulnerabilities. Running containers as root, storing secrets in plain text, or using untrusted images can compromise your system. Security best practices ensure your apps remain safe in production. Always use official or trusted base images. Keep images small to reduce attack surface. Regularly update images. Scan images with tools like Trivy, Clair, or Docker scan. Example: docker scan my_app
Avoid running containers as root. Use a non-root user in your Dockerfile:
RUN addgroup appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup USER appuser
Use resource limits (--memory, --cpus) to avoid resource abuse. Avoid --privileged mode unless absolutely necessary. Never hardcode passwords or API keys in Dockerfiles. Use Docker Secrets (in Swarm) or external secret managers: Docker Secrets AWS Secrets Manager HashiCorp Vault Example (Swarm secret): docker secret create db_password ./db_password.txt docker service create --name db --secret db_password postgres:latest
In Compose (v3.4+), you can define secrets:
secrets: db_password: file: ./db_password.txt
services: db: image: postgres:latest secrets: - db_password
Use custom networks to isolate services. Only expose necessary ports. Consider using firewalls or reverse proxies for additional layers of security. Use trusted base images. Regularly scan images. Run as non-root user. Limit resources. Manage secrets securely. Isolate networks and containers. Scan your app image using Trivy. Run the container as a non-root user. Create a secret and attach it to your container. Test network isolation using custom networks. ✅ Next Episode: Episode 21 — Docker Logging & Monitoring Essentials — learn to keep track of container health and logs in production.

the embeddings look fine, the index builds without errors, but search results come back empty or irrelevant. It’s not because FAISS, pgvector, or Milvus are “broken.”
It’s because the pipeline contracts drift silently: Normalization skipped during ingestion.
Tokenization rules diverge between ingestion and query.
Casing treated inconsistently across environments.
Chunk overlaps misaligned.
Embedding dimensions silently change after a model upgrade.
